title: Mass Raid Prioritisation: Jets First, UAVs After, Unknowns Referred
sub_domain_tag: ground-based air defence — saturation raid engagement sequencing and IFF referral
trigger_conditions: Route a trainee here whenever the presented problem is a simultaneous multi-track raid against a single air-defence site that mixes fast jets with slower UAVs, plus one or more tracks that are not yet classified. Typical trainee phrasings: 'too many targets at once', 'saturation attack', 'mass raid', 'ten inbound', 'drones and jets together', 'which one do I shoot first', 'I only have two rockets in the air', 'both launchers are busy and something is getting close', 'the track is Unknown but it's heading straight at me', 'do I need permission to shoot', 'I think it's friendly but it's acting hostile', 'a drone leaked past me while I was shooting the jets'. Also matches requests about engagement queue management under a two-missiles-in-flight limit, about ordering targets by closure rate rather than by range, and about what to do while waiting for a commander's classification decision on an unknown track.

iff_certainty_levels: Unknown — classification not yet resolved, referral to commander pending

resource_levels.name: Missiles simultaneously in the air (hard system limit)
Commander referral response time for an Unknown track
Hostile tracks in the raid (3 jets, 7 UAVs)
Unclassified tracks entering as Unknown (all actually friendly)

decision_points.situation: The raid appears: three jets and seven UAVs inbound on the site, with three additional tracks entering as Unknown. The lead jet reaches the outer engagement ring and the system displays a valid firing solution against it. Nothing is yet committed; both launchers are free.

valid_actions.label: Fire the lead jet at the earliest valid firing solution
valid_actions.description: Commit a rocket to the fastest closer as soon as the system shows the target inside the envelope with an acceptable kill probability, without waiting for the picture to improve.

valid_actions.label: Hold the jet until it closes to a higher-confidence range
valid_actions.description: Delay commitment to roughly mid-envelope so that kill probability is maximised and fewer rockets are expended per jet.

valid_actions.label: Engage the nearest UAV first, then turn to the jets
valid_actions.description: Clear the closest track on the display first on the reasoning that proximity equals urgency, then handle the jets as they arrive.

valid_actions.label: Wait until all three Unknowns are classified before opening fire at all
valid_actions.description: Resolve the identification picture completely so that no engagement is begun while any ambiguity remains on the display.

decision_points.preferred_action: Fire the lead jet at the earliest valid firing solution
decision_points.rationale: The whole scenario is solvable only if the launchers are free again by the time the UAVs arrive inside the short ring. That is achieved by shooting the jets at the very first moment the system offers a valid solution at long range. The operator's rule is to fire when the system permits it — when the target is within system capability and a solution exists — not to hold for a better picture. Jets are prioritised over UAVs not because they are closer but because they close fastest: they consume the timeline. Every second of delay on a jet commitment is a second the two-rockets-in-the-air limit is still occupied when the UAV wave crosses the short-range ring. Holding for a better shot, or clearing the nearest UAV first, feels tidy but it pushes the jet engagements later and cascades into a broken queue. Waiting for the Unknowns to be resolved before firing at anything confuses two separate problems: identification is referred up in parallel, it is not a gate on engaging tracks already classified Enemy.
common_errors: Engaging the nearest UAV first because proximity reads as urgency on the display, when closure rate — not slant range — is what determines who must die first.
Holding the first jet shot for a better firing solution, which delays launcher availability and guarantees the UAV wave arrives while both rockets are still in the air.
Treating unresolved Unknowns as a reason to withhold all fire, wasting the long-range window in which the jets are cheapest to kill.

decision_points.situation: Both rockets are in the air against jets — the two-in-flight limit is reached — and a UAV crosses the short-range ring. No launcher is available and no fire status has resolved yet.

valid_actions.label: Hold and wait for a fire status to resolve
valid_actions.description: Keep both engagements running, wait for the missiles to report, and take the freed launcher onto the UAV the moment the status resolves.

valid_actions.label: Break one jet engagement to free a launcher for the closing UAV
valid_actions.description: Cease fire on the less-developed jet engagement so that a rocket becomes immediately available against the track now inside the short ring.

valid_actions.label: Switch the guidance of a committed rocket onto the crossing UAV
valid_actions.description: Retarget an in-flight rocket to the nearer, slower track, on the reasoning that the closer threat is the more immediate danger to the site.

valid_actions.label: Salvo a third rocket at the UAV and accept the system limit warning
valid_actions.description: Attempt to exceed the in-flight limit rather than allow a leaker, on the reasoning that a leaked UAV is a guaranteed loss and the limit may be soft.

decision_points.preferred_action: Hold and wait for a fire status to resolve
decision_points.rationale: When both rockets are committed and a UAV crosses the short ring, the correct behaviour is to hold. The timeline is built to be winnable: if the jets were committed at the earliest valid solution, a fire status will resolve in time to take the UAV inside the shorter ring. Panic-switching or ceasing fire on a good engagement throws away a jet kill — the most expensive kind of leaker — in exchange for a UAV that could still have been serviced seconds later. The two-in-flight limit is a hard property of the system, not a suggestion, so trying to force a third launch achieves nothing except lost seconds. The real lesson is that this moment is not where the run is won or lost; it is decided earlier, by how promptly the jets were engaged. If the operator finds this moment genuinely unwinnable, the error is upstream in the queue, not here.
common_errors: Ceasing fire on a developing jet engagement to service a nearer UAV, converting a cheap long-range jet kill into the most costly category of leaker.
Panic-switching an in-flight rocket to the closer track, degrading both engagements and often losing the jet as well as the UAV.
Attempting to exceed the two-rockets-in-the-air limit instead of accepting that the queue must be waited out.
Reading the crossing UAV as evidence that the plan has failed, when it is the expected consequence of a correctly sequenced jet-first engagement.

decision_points.situation: One of the three Unknown tracks is closing on the site, manoeuvring in a way that reads as aggressive. Its classification has not been resolved. The referral to the commander has been made or is available.

valid_actions.label: Refer to the commander and withhold fire until the track is classified Enemy
valid_actions.description: Pass the unknown track up for classification, expect an answer within about fifteen seconds, and hold fire on that track meanwhile while continuing to service classified Enemy tracks.

valid_actions.label: Engage the Unknown on the basis of its aggressive behaviour
valid_actions.description: Treat closing, manoeuvring flight profile as sufficient evidence of hostility and engage before the track reaches a range where it can act.

valid_actions.label: Self-classify the track as Enemy and log the reasoning after the engagement
valid_actions.description: Make the identification call locally to preserve reaction time, on the reasoning that the operator has the best view of the track's behaviour.

valid_actions.label: Ignore the Unknown entirely and give it no further attention
valid_actions.description: Deprioritise the track completely so that attention and launchers stay on confirmed hostiles until the raid is finished.

decision_points.preferred_action: Refer to the commander and withhold fire until the track is classified Enemy
decision_points.rationale: An Unknown is not a permission — it is a question. Classification of unknown tracks is referred up to the commander, who answers in about fifteen seconds, and nothing may be fired on unless it is classified Enemy. Aggressive-looking behaviour is not a classification: in this scenario all three Unknowns are in fact friendly, and the flight profile that reads as threatening is exactly the bait. The fifteen-second referral is short enough that it costs almost nothing against a correctly sequenced engagement queue, so there is no operational justification for self-classifying. Equally, ignoring the track is not the answer: the referral must actually be made, because the same track could come back classified Enemy and then needs to be serviced in its proper place in the queue. The discipline is: refer, keep working the confirmed hostiles, and act on the answer when it arrives.
common_errors: Firing on an Unknown because it behaves aggressively, which is the single worst outcome in this scenario and drives the score down hard regardless of how many hostiles were killed.
Self-classifying an unknown track locally to save the fifteen seconds of referral time, when the referral cost is trivial compared with the consequence of being wrong.
Failing to make the referral at all and simply leaving the track unresolved, so that a track later classified Enemy never enters the engagement queue.
Allowing the Unknown's behaviour to pull attention and launchers off the jets, breaking the sequencing that makes the raid solvable.

decision_points.situation: All three jets have been destroyed or are past the engagement window. Seven UAVs remain, spread across the picture at different ranges, and the two-in-flight limit still applies.

valid_actions.label: Mop up the UAVs by earliest available valid solution inside the shorter rings
valid_actions.description: Work the UAV wave as a continuous queue, launching on whichever UAV has a valid solution each time a launcher frees, keeping both rockets working at all times.

valid_actions.label: Service the UAVs strictly by slant range, nearest first
valid_actions.description: Order the remaining queue purely by distance so that the closest track is always the one being engaged.

valid_actions.label: Hold fire until UAVs enter the innermost part of the envelope to maximise kill probability
valid_actions.description: Conserve rockets by engaging only at short range where solutions are strongest, accepting a tighter timeline per target.

decision_points.preferred_action: Mop up the UAVs by earliest available valid solution inside the shorter rings
decision_points.rationale: Once the fast closers are dealt with, the UAV wave is a throughput problem rather than a prioritisation problem. The operator's rule is unchanged: fire when the system offers a valid solution and the target is within system capability. The objective is to keep both rockets continuously employed so that no UAV reaches a point where no launcher can be brought to bear. Sorting strictly by range is a reasonable instinct but it can idle a launcher while waiting for the nearest track to present a solution; holding for maximum kill probability at short range compresses the remaining timeline and is how leakers happen at the end of a run that was going well. Nothing in this phase overrides the identification rule — any track still Unknown remains off limits until classified Enemy.
common_errors: Idling a launcher while waiting for the nearest UAV to present a solution instead of taking the next available valid shot.
Holding fire for a stronger short-range solution and running out of timeline against the tail of the wave.
Relaxing identification discipline during the mop-up phase and engaging a track that was never classified Enemy.

easy.description: The scenario as specified: ten hostile tracks — three jets and seven UAVs — inbound on the site, plus three tracks entering as Unknown that are in fact friendly. Two rockets may be in the air at once; the commander answers a classification referral in about fifteen seconds. Spacing between the jet and UAV waves is set so that a correctly sequenced run is comfortably winnable.
easy.pressure_note: Recorded as fixed at the expert's explicit instruction ('Don't harden'). The expert's overriding design constraint is that the timeline must be solvable, so the easy tier is simply the specified scenario with generous wave spacing.

medium.description: Identical composition to easy: three jets, seven UAVs, three Unknown tracks, two rockets in the air, fifteen-second commander referral. The reference version of the scenario.
medium.pressure_note: No escalation authorised by the expert. Difficulty is deliberately fixed across tiers; the only variation permitted is modest tightening of wave spacing within the solvable window.

hard.description: Composition unchanged — the expert declined a hardened variant. Three jets, seven UAVs, three Unknown tracks, two rockets in the air, fifteen-second commander referral, with jet and UAV waves at the tightest spacing that still leaves the run winnable if the jets are committed at the earliest valid solution.
hard.pressure_note: Expert instruction was 'Don't harden', so threat count and ambiguity are held constant and this field is intentionally thin. The only pressure lever left in play is wave spacing, and even that is bounded by the requirement that the simulation remain solvable. DESIGNER NOTE: if genuine tiering is later wanted, it must be re-elicited from the expert rather than inferred here.

evaluation_criteria.success_condition: A passing run engages the three jets first, each at the earliest valid firing solution the system offers, then mops up the UAV wave inside the shorter rings; refers every Unknown track to the commander; and fires on nothing that is not classified Enemy. No Unknown or friendly track may be engaged. Holding fire while both rockets are committed, rather than breaking a good engagement, is treated as correct behaviour and not as a failure to act.
evaluation_criteria.scoring_notes: The scoring hierarchy is explicit. Firing on an Unknown is the worst outcome and drives the score down hard, irrespective of how many hostiles were destroyed — a run that kills all ten hostiles but engages an Unknown scores below a run that leaks a target and keeps identification discipline. Among leakers, a jet costs substantially more than a UAV, because the jet is both the harder target to recover and the one whose leakage proves the sequencing was wrong. Some UAV leakage is tolerable in a run that handled the jets first and fired on nothing unclassified. Engagement order is the primary discriminator between a strong run and a mediocre one: two runs that destroy the same number of targets are not equivalent if one took the jets at first valid solution and the other cleared near UAVs first. Breaking or switching a committed engagement under time pressure should be scored as an error even where the outcome happened to be favourable.

source_chat_log:
INTERVIEWER: Let's capture one dilemma an operator of Euro_AD faces. Start anywhere — the situation that makes them hesitate, a decision you have seen go wrong, or the trade-off you most want trainees to feel.

I'll ask follow-up questions as we go, and when there's enough to work with I'll say so.

EXPERT: I want to teach a dilemma of interception of mass of target. Please make 10 targets. 7 uav, 3 jets. That flying towards the ad system. The trainee need to prioritize the shooting, to start with the fast and then the uav. Also plant 3 friends targets that he shouldn’t shoot

INTERVIEWER: That's a clear shape: ten hostiles — three jets and seven UAVs — plus three friendlies in the picture, and the intended lesson is that the jets get shot first because they close fastest, then the UAVs get mopped up inside the shorter rings.

Given the two-rockets-in-the-air limit, the whole exercise is really a queue-management problem. So my first question is about the moment the queue breaks: when the operator has both rockets committed to jets and a UAV is crossing the 20 km short-range ring, what does a good operator actually do — wait for a fire status to resolve, or is there something they should have done earlier so that situation never arose?

EXPERT: He should wait. You need to create the simulation in a way that is possible to solve the situation…

INTERVIEWER: Understood — the timeline has to be winnable, and the correct behaviour when both rockets are committed is to hold and let a fire status resolve rather than panic-switch or cease-fire a good engagement.

So the solvability comes from firing the jets early enough at long range that the launchers are free again by the time the UAVs arrive. Two questions on that: roughly how far out should the operator be committing the first jet — right at the 70 km ring, or does waiting a little improve the picture? And do the three friendlies enter as *Unknown* first, or already classified, since that changes whether the trainee's error is misidentification or impatience?

EXPERT: The operator need to shoot when the system let him, when it is in the system ability. Leave them unknown and let him talk to his commander to decide how to classify them

INTERVIEWER: Good — so the operator fires as soon as the system shows a valid solution (in envelope, acceptable Pk), not holding for a better picture. And the friendlies stay *Unknown* until the operator asks the commander, which is a real addition to what's on file: the profile says nothing about external authority, so I'll record that unknown-track classification is referred up.

Two things about that referral: how long does the commander typically take to answer, and what should the operator do with an Unknown that is closing on the site while the answer hasn't come back yet?

EXPERT: The commander will give answer in 15 seconds . He shouldn’t fire a target that is not an enemy

INTERVIEWER: Clear: a 15-second referral, and no firing on anything not classified Enemy — an Unknown is not a permission, it's a question.

Now the part that makes the debrief worth reading: what do trainees actually get wrong in this scenario? I'd guess two candidates — engaging the nearest UAV first because it looks urgent, or firing on an Unknown that behaves aggressively. Which have you seen, and is there a third?

EXPERT: You are right. No other thing

INTERVIEWER: That covers the errors. Two last things and I think I have it.

For scaling: on the hard version, would you increase the threat count (say twelve to fourteen with more UAVs), shorten the spacing so jets and UAVs arrive nearly together, or add more Unknowns behaving aggressively — and roughly what does an easy run look like by comparison?

And for scoring: is a run a pass only if all ten hostiles are killed and no friendly is fired on, or is some leakage acceptable if the jets were handled first?

EXPERT: Don’t harden.

INTERVIEWER: Fine — no hard variant; the scenario stays as specified, ten hostiles and three Unknowns, and I'll record scaling as fixed rather than inventing tiers.

Last one, then: how is a run scored? Is it pass only if all ten hostiles are destroyed and no Unknown or friendly is engaged, or can a trainee still pass if a UAV leaks through provided the three jets were engaged first and no friendly was fired on?

EXPERT: Killing unknown is bad and punish him with low score. And jet leak is harder then uav

INTERVIEWER: That gives me the scoring hierarchy: firing on an Unknown is the worst outcome and drives the score down hard; a leaked jet costs more than a leaked UAV; and the ordering — jets first at the earliest valid solution, UAVs mopped up after — is what separates a good run from a mediocre one that killed the same number of targets in the wrong order.

I have enough to fill every field. Trigger conditions, key variables, the decision points (first commitment at long range, both rockets committed with a UAV inbound, and the Unknown referral), the errors and the evaluation criteria are all covered; difficulty scaling will be recorded as fixed at your instruction, so that field is deliberately thin rather than missing.
